oneSentence: A number attached to a model’s possible outputs that shows how much of its total estimated likelihood the model assigns to each option.
plainExplanation:
When a model produces several possible outputs, it often also produces numbers for those options. For tasks with mutually exclusive options, these numbers are often turned into probabilities: values between 0 and 1, or 0% and 100%, that add up to 1 across all possible choices. A display may show only some choices, so the displayed values need not add up to 1. The model is not reporting a fact about the world. It is reporting how its calculations distribute likelihood among the options.

What goes in is an input such as text, an image, or sensor data. Inside the model, many numerical steps combine patterns learned from training data. At the end, the model gives raw scores for possible outputs. A method called softmax often converts those scores into probabilities so they can be compared more easily.

What comes out depends on the task. In image classification, the output may be probabilities for labels such as road, tree, or building. In next-word text generation, the output may be probabilities for many possible next tokens, meaning pieces of text. The highest probability often becomes the top suggestion, but systems can also sample from the distribution instead of always picking the top one.

A high probability does not automatically mean the model is correct, safe, or well calibrated. Calibration means whether probabilities match real-world frequencies over many cases. For example, among outputs given 80% probability, about 80% should be right if the system is well calibrated. Output probability is therefore best treated as information about how the model distributes likelihood among options, not as proof.

everydayAnalogy.title: Which bus arrives next?
everydayAnalogy.story: A display predicts that the next bus will be route 4 with 60% probability, route 7 with 30% and route 12 with 10%. The percentages divide the full prediction among the three possibilities, so they add to 100%. Route 4 is the display’s leading guess, but route 7 may still turn the corner first. A high number shows the strength of the prediction relative to the other options, not a promise about what will happen.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A librarian can explain a deliberate search strategy and may use outside knowledge during the search. A model usually produces these numbers through learned numerical patterns, not through a human-style search of shelves. Also, many models assign probabilities over thousands of options at once, not just three neat choices, and the numbers may be poorly calibrated even when the ranking is useful.

visual.title: From input to output probabilities
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that a model first produces raw scores for options, then converts them into probabilities that rank outputs but do not guarantee correctness.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram. An input enters a model, the model produces raw scores for several candidate outputs, and a final stage converts those scores into probabilities that sum to 100%. The reader follows the arrows to see what goes in, what happens inside, and what comes out.

steps.label: 1. Input arrives
steps.explanation: The process starts with one input, such as a sentence or an image.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box on the left labelled 'Input' with an example beneath it, such as 'Photo of a street scene' or 'Text prompt'.

steps.label: 2. Model calculates scores
steps.explanation: The network processes the input and assigns each possible output a raw score. These scores are not yet probabilities.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a middle box labelled 'Model calculations'. Inside, show three output labels with raw scores, for example 'road: 4.2', 'river: 1.1', 'building: 3.0'.

steps.label: 3. Scores become probabilities
steps.explanation: A conversion step, often softmax, turns raw scores into comparable probabilities that add up to 100% across the shown options.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a small box after the model labelled 'Convert to probabilities'. Show the same labels becoming 'road: 73%', 'river: 3%', 'building: 24%'. Add a note 'totals 100%'.

steps.label: 4. System uses the distribution
steps.explanation: The system may choose the top option or may sample from the full distribution. In either case, the numbers express the model’s relative preference among options.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box on the right with two branches: 'Top choice: road' and 'Sampling may choose another option'. Add a caution note below: 'High probability does not equal certainty'.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each stage reveals a one-line note: 'input', 'raw scores', 'probabilities', and 'use in selection'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram shows a four-stage flow from left to right. First, an input such as a photo or text prompt enters the system. Second, the model produces raw scores for several possible outputs, for example road 4.2, river 1.1, building 3.0. Third, a conversion step turns those scores into probabilities, for example road 73%, river 3%, building 24%, with a note that they add up to 100% across the shown options. Fourth, the system either takes the highest-probability option or samples from the distribution. A warning states that high probability does not guarantee the output is correct.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right diagram with four labelled boxes and arrows. The same example scores and probabilities are shown without animation or hover effects.

workedExample.scenario: A programme officer tests a classifier that assigns public, non-confidential project summaries to one of three portal categories.
workedExample.input: A project summary describing drought-resistant crops, local market access and training for small producers.
process: The model produces raw scores for the candidate labels: climate resilience 2.1, livelihoods 1.2 and governance 0.3.
A softmax transformation converts the scores into probabilities of about 66%, 24% and 10%. They are each between 0 and 1 and together sum to 100%.
Using argmax selects climate resilience because it has the highest probability. Sampling could occasionally select livelihoods or governance instead.
workedExample.result: The distribution ranks the three labels for this input. It does not establish that climate resilience is the correct portal category, nor that the 66% figure is a calibrated measure of real-world certainty.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a small field presence with intermittent connectivity, a protection officer must complete a roster screening sheet by close of business. An internal classifier approved for the relevant data assigns each application probabilities across three labels: profile match, needs review and no match.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The probabilities divide the model’s estimated likelihood across the available labels. A 0.72 probability for “profile match” means that label ranks highest under the model, not that the applicant has a 72% chance of being suitable or that the underlying information is correct.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Application material may contain personal or protection-sensitive information. It must not be copied into any tool not explicitly approved for that data, because disclosure could expose applicants to harm. No probability score should be the sole basis for rejecting or deprioritising an application. The officer must review the evidence, the profile criteria and possible model error.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists often see a percentage and assume certainty. That can lead to over-trusting a system, especially when the number only reflects how the model ranks options. Understanding output probability helps you ask better questions: Is this the top guess or just one option among many? Was the model well calibrated? Should a human verify this before it is used in communication, analysis or service delivery? This matters in practice because the same probability can support different actions depending on risk. A spelling suggestion at 70% may be acceptable. A medical, legal, protection or human-rights-related claim at 70% should trigger caution and checking.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model gives 90%, that means there is a 90% chance the statement is true in the real world.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually it means the model assigned more relative likelihood to that output than to the alternatives it considered. Whether 90% corresponds to real-world correctness depends on calibration, the task, the data, and how the options were defined.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Low probability outputs are always useless and should never be chosen.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Low probability only means the model favoured them less. In some systems, exploring lower-probability options can increase variety or surface alternatives. A human may also judge a lower-probability option to be more accurate, fair or context-appropriate.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Probability and accuracy are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Probability is a per-output score about the model’s current preference among options. Accuracy is a broader performance measure comparing outputs with correct answers across many examples. A model can assign high probabilities and still be inaccurate if it is overconfident.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: These numbers show which answers the model leans toward most strongly. They are not guarantees that the top answer is correct.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: For many models, the final layer produces raw values often called logits or scores for candidate outputs. A transformation such as softmax converts these values into a probability distribution over the options, where each probability is between 0 and 1 and the probabilities sum to 1. In classification, this distribution ranks labels. In language models, it ranks possible next tokens at each step. The argmax gives the highest-probability option, while sampling draws from the full distribution. These probabilities are model-based estimates conditioned on the input and the model parameters; they are not automatically calibrated estimates of empirical correctness.

keyTakeaway: An output probability shows how the model divides its estimated likelihood among available options. It ranks those options, but does not by itself prove that the leading one is true or correct.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes a 78% probability attached to one model output?
options: The output is definitely correct in 78 out of 100 future real-world cases.
The model currently favours that output over the listed alternatives, but it may still be wrong.
The model has checked external evidence and confirmed the answer with 78% certainty.
The system’s overall accuracy on all tasks is 78%.
quickCheck.explanation: In most cases, the percentage expresses how the model distributes likelihood across candidate outputs for this input. It is not the same as verified truth, external confirmation, or overall system accuracy. To interpret it well, you also need to know whether the model is calibrated and what task it is performing.

issues.problem: The stated probabilities do not result from applying softmax to the shown raw scores. The arithmetic is: exp(4.2) = 66.6863, exp(1.1) = 3.0042, exp(3.0) = 20.0855, and the sum is 89.7760. Therefore road = 66.6863 / 89.7760 = 74.3%, river = 3.0042 / 89.7760 = 3.3%, and building = 20.0855 / 89.7760 = 22.4%. The page instead gives 73%, 3%, and 24%. If a conversion other than softmax is intended, it must be named.
issues.fix: Replace the probabilities in the visual instruction and accessibility description with 'road: 74.3%', 'river: 3.3%', and 'building: 22.4%'.

issues.problem: The claim that probabilities add up to 1 across the listed choices is false when an interface lists only part of the complete output space. They sum to 1 across a complete set of mutually exclusive possibilities. Displayed top choices may sum to less than 1.
issues.fix: State that probabilities sum to 1 across all possible mutually exclusive choices, while a displayed subset may sum to less than 1.

issues.problem: Saying the model 'considers' possible tokens presents a human mental action as a factual description of model operation.
issues.fix: The model processes the text so far and calculates scores for many possible next tokens.

issues.problem: Several passages reduce probability to a ranking signal. A probability distribution does rank options, but it also states how the model divides probability mass among them. Treating 51% and 99% as merely the same top ranking loses an important part of the concept and weakens the distinction from raw scores or an ordered list.
issues.fix: Describe the values as the model's distribution of probability among options, while retaining the warning that they do not guarantee correctness.
